title: AISA President Neha Bora Refuses Peace Bond, Calls It a Curb on Dissent
excerpt: A day after the Delhi High Court dismissed her plea, the student leader said she will appear before the magistrate on October 29 but will not sign a Rs 10,000 bond for protesting.
body:
• All India Students' Association president Neha Bora said on Saturday she will not sign a peace bond before a special executive magistrate, a day after the Delhi High Court dismissed her challenge to a police notice seeking a personal bond of Rs 10,000 with one surety.
  • The notice, issued October 17 under Section 126 of the BNSS, followed Bora's detention during the 'Lehra Do Tiranga' march demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
  • The High Court did not quash the proceedings, but directed the magistrate to give Bora all material relied on against her and follow natural justice before deciding on a bond; the next hearing is October 29.

All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora said on Saturday that she will not sign a peace bond before a special executive magistrate, questioning how peaceful protest can be treated as a threat to public order, according to The Hindu BusinessLine's PTI report.

"Whose peace am I being asked to keep? If we do not ask the government any questions, whose peace are we keeping?"

— Neha Bora, AISA national president

Addressing the press at the CPI(ML) Liberation office in New Delhi, Bora said demonstrating peacefully on the streets is a democratic right and stressed that the right to question those in power is fundamental to a democracy. She said the fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar must not come at the cost of labelling dissent itself a threat to peace.

What the Notice Asked

The police notice, issued on October 17 under Section 126 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), asked Bora to appear before a special executive magistrate on October 19 and show cause why she should not execute a personal bond of Rs 10,000 with one surety "for keeping peace for a period of inquiry." Section 126 is a preventive provision: it lets a magistrate seek a bond from a person considered likely to breach the peace, before any offence is proved.

The notice came a day after Delhi Police detained Bora as she joined the 'Lehra Do Tiranga' march in the capital, part of protests demanding Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

What the High Court Actually Decided

Bora challenged the notice in the Delhi High Court, arguing the preventive proceedings were an attempt to suppress peaceful dissent and that the notice did not adequately establish a likelihood of a breach of peace. Justice Subramonium Prasad dismissed her petition on October 23 and did not stay the proceedings, holding that sufficient material existed to initiate them, as detailed by eNewsroom's account of the order.

The dismissal came with safeguards. The court directed the State to provide Bora with all material it intends to rely on, and directed the magistrate to ensure natural justice is followed and to assess the material independently — referring to Section 135 of the BNSS and the Supreme Court's Madhu Limaye judgment — before deciding whether any bond is warranted. The court did not rule on the merits of the allegations, which include alleged nuisance at Mandi House and alleged instigation to join an unauthorised demonstration at Connaught Place.

The Other Side

The police and the court's position, in the material examined, is that preventive proceedings rest on more than hearsay: the High Court examined three General Diary entries, a kalandra dated October 17, records of FIRs at Parliament Street, Barakhamba Road and Connaught Place police stations, prohibitory orders under BNSS Section 163, and the magistrate's examination of three witnesses. On that record, the court found enough to let the inquiry proceed — while insisting Bora receive the documents and a fair chance to respond.

AISA, for its part, alleged that a group it described as right-wing supporters threatened Bora outside Mandir Marg Police Station on Saturday as she arrived to appear before the magistrate, and said police brought her inside under protection. The organisation said it will comply with legal procedures but will not sign a bond it believes infringes the right to protest.

What Happens Next

Bora appeared before the magistrate on October 24, the supporting documents were supplied in line with the High Court's directions, and the next hearing is scheduled for October 29. The magistrate must now decide, on the disclosed material, whether a bond is necessary at all — and Bora has made clear that, whatever that decision, she will not sign voluntarily.
